questions.q: How does traffic travel between two peered VNets?
options: Over Microsoft's private backbone network, using private IP addresses — not the public internet
Over the public internet, encrypted by a VPN gateway automatically
Only through ExpressRoute, which is required for any VNet peering
Through a third intermediary VNet that Azure creates automatically
questions.explain: VNet peering routes traffic entirely over Azure's private backbone using private IP addresses, with no VPN or public internet involved.

questions.q: How many peering link objects need to be created to establish a working peering between two VNets?
options: One — peering is automatically bidirectional from a single object
Two — one created on each VNet, each pointing at the other
Three — one on each VNet plus one shared peering resource
Zero — peering is enabled automatically once two VNets share a resource group
questions.explain: VNet peering requires two separate peering link objects, one defined on each VNet, each pointing at the other; both must report Connected for it to work.

questions.q: VNet A peers with a Hub VNet, and the Hub peers with VNet B. Can A reach B directly through that peering chain?
options: No — peering is non-transitive, so A and B have no relationship unless they're explicitly peered with each other too
Yes — any VNet peered to a VNet that is itself peered to another VNet can reach it automatically
Yes, but only if both peerings use the Standard SKU
No — peering chains are limited to a maximum of one hop in the opposite direction
questions.explain: Peering does not chain. A and B have no automatic path through the Hub; they would need an explicit peering between them, or traffic would need to be deliberately routed through the hub.

questions.q: What is the key difference between regional and global VNet peering?
options: Regional peering does not support private IP communication, only global peering does
Regional peering connects VNets in the same Azure region; global peering connects VNets across different regions
Global peering is required whenever more than two VNets are involved
Global peering uses a completely different CLI command than regional peering
questions.explain: Regional peering connects VNets within the same region, while global peering connects VNets across different regions — both use the same command and the same non-transitive behavior.

questions.q: In a hub-and-spoke network design, how do spoke VNets typically communicate with each other?
options: Spoke-to-spoke traffic is routed deliberately through a firewall or network virtual appliance in the hub, using user-defined routes
Spokes cannot communicate with each other under any circumstances
Spokes peer directly with every other spoke in the design
Spoke-to-spoke traffic automatically flows through the hub peering with no additional configuration
questions.explain: Because peering is non-transitive, hub-and-spoke designs route spoke-to-spoke traffic deliberately through a firewall or NVA in the hub using user-defined routes, rather than relying on the hub peering to carry it automatically.
